thirty-three
active Chapters (including Owl Clubs) and more under
graduate members than at any previous time in our history!
What could be a more appropriate time for our Fraternity
to become more involved and interested in the affairs of
other fraternities.
One aspect of Psi U's involvement in the interfraternity
movement is our membership in the National Interfrater
nity Conference. Our attachments go back a long way in
NIC �
all the way back to the late thirties when Scott
Turner, our own past President, was the President of NIC.
His own distress upon Psi U's departure from NIC in the
mid-part of this century did not deter Psi U from re-entering
NIC in the 1970's and the active involvement of Brother
Poor and Brothers Morey and McShane since that time. My
first opportunity to see the NIC in action was at its annual
meeting in Louisville last December. I was delighted at the
willingness to share experiences and information that ex
isted there and made many friendships that merely extend
the group of "brothers
"
to whom we may all turn for as
sistance.
My experience was so encouraging that I was able to
persuade the Executive Council to hold its meeting this
December in Washington in conjunction with the annual
meeting of NIC on December 5-7, 1985, at the Hyatt Re
gency Crystal City near Washington National Airport. This
effort to participate with other fraternity volunteers and
executives was a superb opportunity for our own volunteer
leaders to exchange information with other fraternity leaders
and gain new ideas in ways to deal with "the same old
problems."
Our interfraternity efforts are not limited to the annual
meeting of the National Interfraternity Conference, you can
be sure. Brother Poor is an active member of the Fraternity
Executives Association, having served as its President in
recent years and the current chairman ofa task force to plan
for rather than react to circumstances similar to those that
have occurred at Amherst College and Colby College in
recent years. In addition. Brother Poor has been asked in
recent years to assist in visits to various college and uni
versity campuses for the purpose of reviewing the fraternity
systems and making recommendations to the administration
and interfraternity councils for improvements.
Our field directors have regularly attended National Field
Staff Conferences sponsored by the NIC to orient new
fraternity field men to their jobs. That training, combined
with a
unique opportunity to have our field directors trained
by the staff of Lambda Chi Alpha, has given them a rare
insight into how other fraternities operate and how that can
best be utilized by Psi U in its ongoing operations.
In addition to these disparate activities. Brother Poor and
I have also had several unique opportunities to participate
in planning for the future of the fraternity movement. He
has participated for the last several years in several seminars
designed to look at new
approaches to the fraternity ex
perience, not only from the specific fraternity viewpoint but
also from the university and business viewpoint as well. I
had a recent opportunity to participate in a conference spon
sored by NIC to assist in the long range planning for that
organization. Bringing together national fraternity and so
rority presidents and executives as well as
fraternity advis
ers, student affairs deans and vice presidents, and finally
college and university presidents themselves to plan for the
future of the fraternity movement is quite an exciting ex
perience. Breaking down into small groups carefully crafted
to include members of all groups represented, we prog
nosticated about the next twenty-five years, looked at what
the challenges and successes will be, and tried to identify
appropriate organizational mechanisms to best meet those
challenges. Those of you who have participataed in corpo
rate or governmental long range planning processes will
understand both the enjoyment and the frustration of at
tempting to "crystal ball" the future while still trying to
keep your feet planted firmly in the present. It is certainly
a
mind-expanding experience, and one that may prove help
ful to Psi U as well.
Our interfraternity involvement is not limited to events
involving many fraternities and multiple groups of con
cerned parties. We have also been working closer to home
to reactivate an old interfraternity association �
the His
torical Triad. This group of three fraternities �
Psi Upsilon,
Alpha Delta Phi, and Delta Kappa Epsilon �
holds a long
historical thread! We have attempted to rekindle this old
association with two meetings in the spring and summer of
this year to share common challenges and experiences rang
ing from education programs to foundations to annual giving
and see where our common interests might lead us.
In short, Psi U has always been involved in interfratemity
efforts, whether it be encouraging the continuing involve
ment of our
undergraduate Chapters in the interfraternity
council on their campus, working with a few national fra
ternities with whom we share a special heritage, or making
some small contribution (and taking away a wealth of ex
perience and information) within the National Interfrater
nity Conference or the Fraternity Executives Association.
Our efforts will continue and, we hope, will reap great new
opportunities for Psi U to face the future better armed than
we have been in the past.
Yours in the Bonds,
William R . Robie
President
Epsilon Omega '66

Annual Giving Program
Unce again the loyal and generous alumni of Psi Up
silon have come through with flying colors! The 1984-85
Annual Giving goal of $135,200 seemed very ambitious,
for it represented an increase of almost $19,000 overthe
previous year's results. But that goal was met, even
exceeded by over $6,000!
The 1984-85 Annual Giving program resulted in
2,273 contributionstotaling $141,505. This represents
an average gift size of $62.26, probably the highest in
the fraternity world and over $10 larger than last year's
average gift. A major factor in this dramatic growth was
the increase in leadership contributors (those giving $50
or more) from 821 in 1983-84 to 989 in 1984-85.
This response is truly heartwarming, for it has allowed
the Fraternity to meet the always escalating cost of pro
viding comprehensive service to all its members, espe
cially to our undergraduate Chapters, thus ensuring Psi
Upsilon's continued stability and strength.
The following statistics and lists, which represent gifts
received from July 1, 1984 through June 30, 1985 (gifts
received subsequent to June 30 have been credited to
1985-86), serve to honor the faithful and supportive
members of Psi Upsilon who, by their generosity, have
enabled the Fraternity to continue on its distinguished
course. The Executive Council is deeply and profoundly
grateful for each measure of assistance, large and small.
